## THE SWIFTDISC by Brian Gaff

Here are my views on the current SWIFTDISC, with ref. to what I know about the new version.

The old system sits under the Speccy like IF 1 does, while the new model looks like a Joystick I/F. All further comments apply to the old version unless otherwise stated.

There are two ways of using the system. You can use it with its own syntax which is of the form:

`LOAD%0;"filename"`

or from the magic button. In this mode the commands are single letters. However, only image files can be loaded this way. Image files? These are programs saved by the button. You can save any program this way, very much like having a built in Multiface. Disc capacity is high. It is around 720k, though it is not given directly.

A CAT only gives free space in a 'Free Disc Blocks' format. On the button type SAVEs, the system can tell if it is a 128k or a 48k SAVE. However, you must be careful not to try to reload 48k image files into 128k mode & vice versa!

Next we come to the Emulator. This is about £13's worth of software that makes a disc drive into 4 microdrives! This is an emulation and although it works with Basic there are some pitfalls.

The main one is that any s/ware that calls IF1 hardware directly is unlikely to work. If it uses the hook codes you should be OK. The new version can have an optional hardware emulator fitted that helps with this. It will also cure the need to replace IF1's `CLOSE#` with `CLOSE#%#` when using the old version. Oddly the error that causes this is in the old Speccy ROM CLOSE routine!

The button does NOT function in emulator mode, but on the new version it will. The emulator gives you 127k per drive but is slower than the Swift's own operating system.

It does have an RS232, but this is output only & used a weird edge card. The new version will have a lead mounted plug & can be adapted to have a Centronics port instead. There is a Kempston Joystick port as well.

Faults? It can be prone to crashing with mains interference. This problem is being investigated by the makers now. It will run with IF1 fitted, but becomes less reliable the further away from the Speccy it gets. The new model is much better in this respect.

*Brian Gaff*

---

Thanks Brian. Although I've not used the SWIFTDISC I've got a bit of info here I may as well add on to what you've said...

Apart from microdrive emulation, Interface 1 and microdrives can be used with the SWIFTDISC thus enabling direct data transfer between microdrive and disk.

There is a through port so you can add on other perifer- er, perfiph - you can plug in other hardware.

A 48K program will LOAD in under 6 seconds.

The SWIFTDISC uses NO Spectrum memory or I/O.

The address I have here if you want more details is:

```text
SIXWORD LTD. 26 CHURCH ROAD,
WARSASH, SOUTHAMPTON SO3 6GD
```

I must stress that the info I've added is just copied off one of their own leaflets.

Now I'll say a bit about the Opus Discovery. Anyone else who'd like to send in their own views and information about their own systems or any hardware they use will be more than welcome. I feel info from several users is worth more than one review as different people emphasise different areas of the same thing.

This is not intended to be an exhaustive review but just to give some impressions to compare with microdrives which is my other system.

Physically, the Discovery is one unit — the disc drive(s) and the operating system in one unit. I have a double drive in one unit.

The single drive system is the same unit with the right-hand disc slot shielded off. An extra drive can then be added later.

The Discovery has a flat metal plate at the front on which the Spectrum sits. I'm still using an old 48K rubber-keyed Spectrum with that set-up and yet there is very little room to maneouvre the connections between the Opus and the Spectrum so I'm not sure how easy it would be to attach later versions of the Spectrum. A screw underneath prevents the thing coming apart and you are supposed to switch off at the mains if disconnecting the two so you have to make sure all the other plugs — the TV, earphone etc. are properly working as you can't remove them once it's all connected. The Spectrum takes its power from the Opus so you don't need to connect the 9V plug or have a second power plug in use.

There's an on-off switch at the back and at the right-hand side is a through port, a centronics printer port and a Kempston joystick port. Note that the Alphacom printer will not normally work with the Opus for some reason (although I've heard that some users seem to have them working together).

CAT is like on the microdrives but by comparison, very, very fast — there's no waiting at all to speak of because the CAT info is kept in a special file on the disc all ready for the system to read. A normal disc always gives 178K free after a FORMAT.

One niggling problem which seems like a design fault to me is that if you accidentally use a drive without the disc in, the drive continues to go round (you can just hear it) but there is nothing to indicate this on the screen. If you were hard of hearing you would never know. It may be that it doesn't matter at all — certainly it's never caused me any problems but I don't fancy going out of the room and coming back hours later to find it's still running. Use of STOP makes no difference and the only way to stop the motor going round (apart from switching off and what will that do to the system?) is to do an operation like CAT on the other drive and when it's finished it stops the other motor as well. If you only have one drive I've heard you can just push a disc in with no harm but I find it a little bit worrying. Incidentally, the drives do not make much noise in operation although there is an intermittent vibrating sound (as the recording head moves back across the disc I guess) which I think is common to many disc drives. Mind you, I wouldn't have thought it would be a difficult engineering feat to dampen whatever it is that judders!

As well as CAT — LOAD, SAVE and particularly ERASE are faster than microdrives. For shorter files, ERASE is instant. ZAP, in Issue 9 gives the approximate time to ERASE a sequence of files in minutes. For the Opus version I had to re-calibrate it in SECONDS! Actually about 20 times faster by my estimate. The time taken to load a typical issue of OUTLET from "run" to the appearance of the CONTENTS page is about two thirds of the time taken with a microdrive but then occasionly, if a cartridge was just stopped at the start of the "run" file it will load in a similar time. I get the feeling that actual transfer of data is about the same but ACCESSING the data, i.e. finding the start of a program on cartridge or disc or finding a place to SAVE data is much faster on the Discovery. So, the faster access of the Discovery is not so noticeable when loading VERY large programs as most of the time taken is in transferring data after it has been found.

One of the reasons for the speed of the Opus is that each program is saved on sectors of the disc that are together in sequence whereas the microdrive may have to load bits of a program from odd sectors all over the place. One disadvantage is that you can have a disc with 20K free — but spread around with 2K here, 5K there — amongst all the other programs. In such a case, a 10K program say, will not SAVE unless there is 10K free in CONSECUTIVE sectors. Even if there is 20K free, it is not all in one place on the disc! The cure is to "compact" the disc using the MOVE command. This shuffles all the programs on a disc together so all the spare space is moved to the end. Just a minor niggle when you're doing ten things at once and want to SAVE something in a hurry!

Microdrive syntax can be used unchanged or you can abbreviate it to e.g. `SAVE *1;"name"`, i.e. drop the "m" bit which saves a bit of typing.

"run" files load automatically like on microdrive and this will still work (unlike the mdrive) even if you have entered some direct commands after a re-set. So long as there are no program lines in BASIC, RUN and ENTER will LOAD a "run" file.

There's more comprehensive file-handling with random-access of data files etc. but I've not had chance to explore this area.

Copying files about is easy with the MOVE command and you can re-name the file while you're at if you want. It's also easy to copy a whole disc to another disc in a minute or two (although if you only have one drive you will have to switch discs a few times during the operation).

Part of the Spectrum's memory may be set aside as a RAM DISC if you want for temporary rapid access of programs and data.
